text.p: Former "Bandit Queen" Phoolan Devi, who was wanted by police in dozens of criminal cases including murder, ended weeks of seclusion on Monday to attend India's parliament, where she is a lawmaker.
"There is no warrant against me. Why should I surrender?" Devi told reporters at the gate of Parliament House.
The Allahabad high court in the northern Indian state of Uttar Pradesh had on February 20 deferred an arrest warrant pending against Devi on 57 charges until March 20.

Earlier, police, who were searching for Devi on the basis of a court warrant, had said they would arrest her if she arrived in parliament. Parliament began its budget session the day Devi obtained the temporary abeyance of her arrest.
Clad in a green sari, Devi quietly entered the lower house, the Lok Sabha, and sat in a back row. Other lawmakers did not appear to take notice of her and went about business as usual.
Umed Singh Kashyap, Devi's husband, told Reuters in the Parliament House that she would function normally as a deputy in view of the month's time she had gained in the high court.
"She has no problem. She will keep on coming to the parliament," Kashyap said.
He said India's Supreme Court was expected to consider an appeal on February 28 by the Uttar Pradesh state government seeking the withdrawal of all pending cases against Devi.
"We are ready to face the cases. We are confident of getting justice," Kashyap said.
Asked why Devi had evaded arrest for the past few weeks, Kashyap said she was unwell and recovering in a hospital.
"The lawyer was representing her," he said.
Devi was portrayed by director Shekhar Kapur in the film "Bandit Queen" as a rape victim from a low caste community of boatmen whose career of crime began as a search for revenge on her attackers.

She rose to notoriety in 1981 when 22 upper caste men were massacred in the northern Indian village of Behmai. She denied leading the killers but surrendered to police in the central state of Madhya Pradesh in 1983.
Devi was released on parole in 1994 after India's Supreme Court said she had already spent several years in detention.
The government in her home state of Uttar Pradesh dropped charges against her, and its ruling regional socialist party, which represents low castes, enlisted her as a member.
Last year, she contested and won a seat in the federal parliament.
But she faced police action again after the state's high court revived charges against her at the request of a man who says he was one of her intended victims.
A court in the industrial town of Kanpur issued a warrant for police to arrest her.
